result: MEP glia originate from nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors in the lateral floor plate of the spinal cord. These precursors express both CNS markers (nkx2.2a, olig2) and PNS markers (foxd3, sox10), and maintain expression of both marker types once in the PNS. The cells have morphology and position reminiscent of radial glia and express GFAP.
evaluation: Claims C3, C24, C25, C41, C43, C48, C57-C64 are supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including live imaging (Figure 1B-F, Figure 2A-C), marker expression analysis (Figure 1G-I), immunohistochemistry (Figure 2D), and in situ hybridization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D). The identification of nkx2.2a as a new marker for MEP glia is well-documented through imaging at multiple developmental stages. The conclusion that MEP glia originate from lateral floor plate nkx2.2a+/olig2+ radial glial precursors is supported by co-expression analysis and morphological observations.

result: Foxd3 is required for MEP glia to delaminate from the lateral floor plate and exit the spinal cord. In foxd3-/- larvae, MEP glia are specified and express Sox10 but remain in the ventral spinal cord and fail to migrate into the periphery. Foxd3 expression precedes Sox10 expression in MEP glia, and Sox10 expression is independent of foxd3. MEP glia delaminate in a foxd3-dependent manner analogous to neural crest cell delamination.
evaluation: Claims C4, C25, C65-C88 are strongly supported by time-lapse imaging (Figure 3A, Videos 1-2), quantitative analysis (Figure 3C-D), in situ hybridization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), immunohistochemistry (Figure 3F), and temporal expression analysis (Figure 3G). The foxd3 mutant phenotype is well-characterized showing MEP glia specification occurs but delamination and exit fail. The conclusion that foxd3 is required for delamination but not specification is supported by multiple independent assays including wif1 expression and Sox10 immunostaining.

result: Overexpression of foxd3 is sufficient to generate supernumerary MEP glia-like cells in the CNS that eventually exit the spinal cord at MEP TZs. This demonstrates that foxd3 can induce delamination of MEP glia from the lateral floor plate.
evaluation: Claims C85-C88 are supported by foxd3 mRNA injection experiments with imaging data (Figure 3H-I) and time-lapse imaging (Video 4). The observation of supernumerary nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ cells in the CNS that exit through MEP TZs provides gain-of-function evidence complementing the loss-of-function foxd3 mutant data. The analogy to neural crest cell delamination is supported by citation to previous work in chick (C85).

result: MEP glial exit from the spinal cord requires matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). Inhibition of MMPs with GM6001 prevents MEP glia from crossing the CNS/PNS boundary, phenocopying the foxd3 mutant. Mmp17b and adamts3 are expressed in the ventral neural tube prior to MEP glial exit, and adamts3 expression is reduced in foxd3-/- embryos.
evaluation: Claims C89-C101 are supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments (Figure 4A-D, Videos 5-6), quantitative analysis (Figure 4B-C), and in situ hybridization (Figure 4E). The GM6001 treatment experiments show that MMP inhibition blocks MEP glial migration out of the spinal cord with quantitative data showing 90.61% exit in controls vs 8.58% in treated embryos at 55 hpf. The identification of adamts3 as a potential downstream target of foxd3 is supported by expression analysis, though the lack of effect of adamts3 overexpression (C101) suggests additional factors are involved.

result: Neural tube precursors give rise to a single MEP glial progenitor cell per hemi-segment that exits the CNS and divides to populate motor nerve roots. Lineage tracing using Zebrabow shows 96.67% of MEP glia along a single motor nerve originated from the same nkx2.2a+ precursor. MEP glia proliferate between 50-56 hpf (74% EdU+) and undergo 1-4 cell divisions to generate up to 6 cells per nerve by 4 dpf. Some MEP glia maintain progenitor markers (sox2, BLBP).
evaluation: Claims C102-C116 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including lineage tracing (Figure 5A-C), EdU incorporation assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C), time-lapse imaging quantification (Figure 5D), cell cycle arrest experiments (Figure 5E-F), and progenitor marker expression (Figure 5G-H). The Zebrabow clonal analysis provides strong evidence that MEP glia along the same nerve share a common progenitor (96.67% same color). The cell cycle arrest experiments showing only one MEP glia per hemi-segment when proliferation is blocked (Figure 5E-F) directly support the single progenitor model.

result: Spinal motor axons are necessary and sufficient to drive MEP glial migration into the PNS. In plexinA3 mutants with ectopic motor exit points, MEP glia are present along all motor nerves including ectopic ones. When motor neurons are genetically ablated using hb9:yfp-ntr and metronidazole, MEP glia fail to exit the spinal cord but are specified (wif1+ cells remain in CNS).
evaluation: Claims C117-C125 are supported by experiments in plexinA3 mutants (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B) and motor neuron ablation experiments (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B). The presence of MEP glia along ectopic motor nerves in plexinA3 mutants demonstrates sufficiency of motor axons. The motor neuron ablation experiments showing MEP glia remain in the CNS (wif1+ and foxd3+ cells detected in spinal cord but not PNS) demonstrate necessity of motor axons. Controls showing normal OPC and Schwann cell development rule out non-specific effects.

result: Neuregulin1 type III (nrg1) expressed on motor axons drives MEP glial migration to motor roots. In nrg1-/- and erbb3b mutants, MEP glia and Schwann cells are absent from motor nerve roots. MEP glia exit the spinal cord in nrg1 mutants but fail to associate with motor root axons and migrate away (wif1+ cells found distally near lateral line nerve). OPC processes extend into the PNS in nrg1 mutants.
evaluation: Claims C126-C140 are supported by analysis of nrg1-/- and erbb3b mutants using photoconversion (Figure 7A), in situ hybridization (Figure 7B-C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B), and citations to previous work. The observation that MEP glia exit the spinal cord but migrate away from motor roots in nrg1 mutants (wif1+ cells found distally) demonstrates nrg1 is required for directed migration rather than exit per se. The similar phenotype in erbb3b mutants supports the conclusion that nrg1 signals through erbb3b receptors.

result: Overexpression of neuregulin1 type III in CNS neurons is sufficient to generate additional MEP glia from nkx2.2a+ radial glial precursors in the post-embryonic spinal cord. Nrg1 overexpression increases proliferation of ventral spinal cord PH3+/nkx2.2a+ cells and increases the total number of MEP glia along motor nerves. Sox2+/nkx2.2a+ radial glial progenitors persist in the spinal cord at 4 dpf, suggesting nrg1 can control their proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C141-C150 are supported by neuregulin overexpression experiments using neuroD:gal4;UAS:hNrg1 larvae with in situ hybridization (Figure 8A), live imaging (Figure 8B-C), immunohistochemistry (Figure 8D-F), and EdU incorporation assays (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B-C). The observation of additional nkx2.2a+/foxd3+ MEP glia in the ventral spinal cord (Figure 8B-C) and increased PH3+/nkx2.2a+ proliferating cells (Figure 8D-E) supports the conclusion that nrg1 regulates MEP glial progenitor proliferation. The detection of Sox2+/nkx2.2a+ cells at 4 dpf (Figure 8F) supports the conclusion that radial glial precursors persist in post-embryonic development.

result: Ventral spinal cord precursors employ neural crest cell (NCC) developmental mechanisms to generate hybrid, peripheral myelinating glia.
evaluation: Claim C29 is a high-level conclusion supported by the collective evidence from multiple experiments. The use of foxd3 for delamination (analogous to NCCs), requirement for MMPs for migration through the CNS/PNS boundary, dependence on axonal neuregulin signaling (similar to Schwann cells), and expression of both CNS and PNS markers all support this conclusion. This represents an integration of the major findings rather than a single experimental result.

result: MEP glia transiently express olig2 until approximately 55 hpf with dramatically diminished GFP fluorescence after exiting the spinal cord. Olig2-driven eGFP levels in MEP glia are 4.18 times lower than pMN domain cells and 7.68 times lower than OPCs at 55 hpf. In situ hybridization shows no olig2+ cell bodies in the PNS at 48 or 72 hpf. In contrast, nkx2.2a-driven GFP fluorescence remains stable after MEP glial exit. The olig2 pMN domain and nkx2.2a lateral floor plate merge to form a mixed domain by 48 hpf.
evaluation: Claims C44, C49-C56 are supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements (Figure 1G-I), time course analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C), in situ hybridization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and imaging of neural tube sections (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). The quantitative data clearly show differential regulation of olig2 vs nkx2.2a expression in MEP glia. The observation that the pMN and lateral floor plate domains merge by 48 hpf is consistent with previous literature on OPC specification.

result: Background and context claims establishing the known biology of oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, MEP glia, neural tube organization, and the knowledge gaps addressed by the study.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C7-C23, C30-C40 are primarily background knowledge claims supported by citations to previous literature. These establish the context for the study including: (1) the known functions of oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells, (2) the previous identification of MEP glia by the authors, (3) the organization of the neural tube, (4) the knowledge gaps regarding MEP glial origin and development. These claims are well-supported by appropriate citations and provide necessary context for interpreting the new findings.

result: At 72 hpf and 4 dpf, both nkx2.2a+/sox10+ MEP glia and nkx2.2a+/sox10- perineurial glia are observed along motor nerve axons. MEP glial membrane sheaths are reminiscent of myelin internodes, while perineurial cell membranes are loose. Mbp+ myelin sheaths are formed by foxd3+ cells along motor root axons at 4 dpf.
evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by imaging data (Figure 1D-F) showing the morphological and molecular distinctions between MEP glia and perineurial glia. The observations are consistent with previous characterization of these cell types and provide additional marker information (nkx2.2a) to distinguish them.

result: One foxd3+ cell is consistently detected in the ventral spinal cord per hemi-segment of the zebrafish trunk.
evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by consistent observations across multiple imaging experiments (Figure 1B, Figure 2A-B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This observation is important for establishing the single progenitor model but is a descriptive finding rather than a mechanistic result.
